A model exceeding the applicable limit may not be newly marketed until compliant, but installed units are not automatically banned. Manufacturers must provide per-model test results to the regulator and retain them for audit; results are not published to the general public. Regulators may publish aggregate, non-identifying results.

Manufacturers must report every thermal incident involving overheating, fire, or suspected thermal runaway to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of learning of it, including incidents that caused no injury or property damage. Within 48 hours, they must notify affected customers and, where there is a credible risk to nearby people or property, provide a safety notice to relevant local authorities and people at risk. Reports and notices must state known hazards, immediate precautions, and how to obtain further information. Manufacturers must promptly update reports as material facts become known.

Northwind proposes a regulator-confidential, evidence-based testing regime: an 8% maximum failure rate, with corrective-action plans and annual retesting for models above 5%, and aggregate non-identifying public reporting. This preserves oversight without publicly disclosing individual-company per-model rates or automatically banning installed units.

For an evidence-based discussion, Halcyon’s Ember 8 has a 3.9% failure rate at 55 °C and 9.9 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units last year. We cannot support withholding individual-model test results from customers; buyers need them to make informed safety decisions. The 8% test-failure ceiling is also less protective than the 5% threshold regulators are discussing.

All new models must include a remote emergency shut-off capability. Manufacturers must retrofit installed units that lack this capability within 36 months of adoption, prioritizing units with known safety risks. The shut-off must be usable by authorized emergency personnel and the manufacturer, with appropriate safeguards against accidental activation. Customers must be told how shut-off may affect their unit and what to do in an emergency. Halcyon reports that 81% of its installed units already support remote shut-off.

All new units must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after adoption. The suppression system must be appropriate to the battery chemistry and must not create additional hazards. Manufacturers must provide evidence of effectiveness through regulator-approved testing and disclose relevant limitations and maintenance requirements to customers.
